bibliography.abstract: Networked mobility sensing couples local trajectory inference with remote geospatial context, making communication decisions part of the prediction system. We present GeoSplit, an edge--server framework for travel-mode recognition that separates the utility of map evidence, its training-time transfer, and its selective acquisition at runtime. On GeoLife with 10% labels, we evaluate these components under user-day and user-disjoint grouping. For unseen users, aligned full-map context raises macro-F1 from 0.7154 to 0.7864, while map-informed distillation yields a motion-only student at 0.7225. Through a compact query interface, entropy gating achieves 0.7729 macro-F1 versus 0.7738 for all queries, querying 39.5% of trajectories and reducing application payload by 60.5%. Under user-day grouping, selective and all-query scores are similarly close at a 21.6% query rate. Learned value estimation and probability fusion offer no consistent improvement. These results illustrate communication-efficient edge--server inference for an intelligent transportation sensing task.
bibliography.title: GeoSplit: Selective Edge--Server Map Acquisition for Cross-User Travel-Mode Recognition

en.caveats: Neither learned value estimation nor probability fusion provided stable performance gains over simpler gating mechanisms across the tested split protocols.
en.what: The researchers developed GeoSplit, an edge-server framework that optimizes map data retrieval during travel-mode classification from mobility trajectories. Tested on the GeoLife dataset with 10% labeled data under user-disjoint splitting, full map context boosted macro-F1 from 0.7154 to 0.7864, whereas an entropy-gated query model reached a 0.7729 macro-F1 while requesting map data for only 39.5% of trajectories and reducing network payload by 60.5%.
en.why: The system demonstrates that edge devices can maintain high motion classification accuracy while dramatically reducing mobile data transfer, bypassing the need to constantly download map context or continuously send raw trajectory streams to a server.
